title: Αἴας ἀναχωρῶν
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Zeus fills Ajax with fear, and he backs away from the Trojans like a lion driven from the cattle-yard, and like a stubborn ass that boys cannot beat out of a field of grain, while the Trojans and their allies keep stabbing at his shield. Eurypylus comes up and spears Apisaon, but as he strips the body Alexander shoots him in the thigh. Wounded, he calls on the Argive leaders to stand round Ajax, and Ajax turns back to meet them. Achilles, watching from the stern of his ship, sees Nestor’s horses carrying a wounded man out of the fighting and sends Patroclus to find out who it is. At Nestor’s hut Hecamede, the captive woman Nestor won at Tenedos, sets out a table and stirs a drink of wine, goat’s cheese and barley-meal in the old man’s great cup. Patroclus arrives, but will not sit: he has seen that the wounded man is Machaon, and he must hurry back to Achilles, whom he describes to Nestor as a dread man who might blame even the blameless.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δὲ πατὴρ Αἴανθ’ ὑψίζυγος ἐν φόβον ὦρσε·
sentences.tr: Zeus de patēr Aianth’ hypsizygos en phobon ōrse·
sentences.l: And Zeus the father, sitting on high, in Ajax fear stirred up;
sentences.i: Then Zeus the father, who sits on high, stirred up fear in Ajax;
sentences.n: Zeus now acts on Ajax. ὑψίζυγος ‘sitting on high’ is Zeus’ epithet (ὕψι ‘on high’ + ζυγόν ‘bench, seat’), and Αἴανθ’ is the accusative Αἴαντα ‘Ajax’ with its final vowel elided, the τ becoming θ before the rough breathing of ὑψίζυγος. ἐν … ὦρσε is tmesis, the preverb ἐν ‘in’ standing apart from ὦρσε, the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘stir up’; φόβον ‘fear’ is what is stirred up, and Ajax is the man it is stirred up in.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ ταφών, ὄπιθεν δὲ σάκος βάλεν ἑπταβόειον,
τρέσσε δὲ παπτήνας ἐφ’ ὁμίλου θηρὶ ἐοικὼς
ἐντροπαλιζόμενος ὀλίγον γόνυ γουνὸς ἀμείβων.
sentences.tr:
stē de taphōn, opithen de sakos balen heptaboeion,
tresse de paptēnas eph’ homilou thēri eoikōs
entropalizomenos oligon gony gounos ameibōn.
sentences.l:
And he stood, amazed, and behind him he cast the seven-hided shield,
and he trembled, glancing about at the throng, like a wild beast,
turning back again and again, a little, knee for knee changing.
sentences.i: He stood in amazement and cast the seven-hided shield behind him; he flinched, glancing about at the throng, like a wild beast, turning to look back again and again as he moved a little at a time, one knee passing the other.
sentences.n: Ajax gives way. ταφών ‘amazed’ is the aorist participle of the verb that goes with τέθηπα ‘be astounded’ and τάφος ‘amazement’. βάλεν is the aorist of βάλλω without its augment (Attic ἔβαλεν); σάκος … ἑπταβόειον is the ‘seven-hided’ shield, seven layers of ox-hide (βόειος ‘of an ox’), and ὄπιθεν ‘behind’ says only that the shield goes behind him, not why. τρέσσε is a past tense of τρέω ‘tremble, flee in fear’ (the verb covers both, and what follows is a slow backing away), and ἐφ’ ὁμίλου is ‘at the throng’. θηρὶ ἐοικώς ‘like a wild beast’ is the perfect participle of ἔοικα with the dative. ἐντροπαλιζόμενος ‘turning back again and again’ is built on ἐν + τρέπω with a repeating force; ὀλίγον ‘a little’ is adverbial, and γόνυ γουνὸς ἀμείβων ‘changing knee for knee’ is one knee passing the other.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ αἴθωνα λέοντα βοῶν ἀπὸ μεσσαύλοιο
ἐσσεύαντο κύνες τε καὶ ἀνέρες ἀγροιῶται,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ aithōna leonta boōn apo messauloio
esseuanto kynes te kai aneres agroiōtai,
sentences.l:
And as a fire-bright lion from the cattle’s farmyard
dogs and men, countrymen, have driven off,
sentences.i: As when dogs and countrymen drive a fire-bright lion away from the cattle’s farmyard,
sentences.n: A simile begins; its comparison with Ajax comes at 556. ὡς δ’ ‘and as’ opens it, and the aorist ἐσσεύαντο ‘have driven off’ is the aorist of a simile, which states what happens every time (the English uses the present). It is the middle of σεύω ‘drive, chase’, with the doubled σ after the augment, and the lion (αἴθωνα, ‘fire-bright’, the word the table keeps for αἴθων) is its object. μεσσαύλοιο is the genitive of μέσσαυλος, the yard inside a farmstead, and βοῶν is the genitive plural of βοῦς ‘cattle’. ἀνέρες is the Homeric form of ἄνδρες, and ἀγροιῶται ‘countrymen’ are the men of the farms.

sentences.t:
οἵ τέ μιν οὐκ εἰῶσι βοῶν ἐκ πῖαρ ἑλέσθαι
πάννυχοι ἐγρήσσοντες·
sentences.tr:
hoi te min ouk eiōsi boōn ek piar helesthai
pannychoi egrēssontes·
sentences.l:
who do not let him take the fat from the cattle,
all night keeping awake;
sentences.i: and these, keeping awake all night, will not let him take the fat of the cattle;
sentences.n: The relative clause tells what the dogs and countrymen do. οἵ τε ‘who’ has the epic τε; εἰῶσι is the present of ἐάω ‘allow’ in its epic form, and μιν ‘him’ is the lion. πῖαρ is ‘fat’, here the rich flesh of the cattle (ἑλέσθαι ‘to take’ has it as object), and βοῶν ἐκ is ‘from the cattle’. πάννυχοι ‘all night through’ and ἐγρήσσοντες ‘keeping awake’ (participle of ἐγρήσσω) describe the men.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ κρειῶν ἐρατίζων
ἰθύει, ἀλλ’ οὔ τι πρήσσει·
sentences.tr:
ho de kreiōn eratizōn
ithyei, all’ ou ti prēssei·
sentences.l:
but he, for flesh longing,
charges straight on, but accomplishes nothing;
sentences.i: But he, longing for flesh, charges straight on, but accomplishes nothing;
sentences.n: The lion in the simile. κρειῶν is the Homeric genitive plural of κρέας ‘flesh’, and ἐρατίζων ‘longing for’ takes the genitive. ἰθύει is ‘charges straight on’ (from ἰθύς ‘straight’), and οὔ τι πρήσσει ‘accomplishes nothing’ (πρήσσω ‘accomplish’).

sentences.t:
θαμέες γὰρ ἄκοντες
ἀντίον ἀΐσσουσι θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν
καιόμεναί τε δεταί, τάς τε τρεῖ ἐσσύμενός περ·
sentences.tr:
thamees gar akontes
antion aïssousi thraseiaōn apo cheirōn
kaiomenai te detai, tas te trei essymenos per·
sentences.i: for close-set javelins fly against him from bold hands, and so do burning torches, from which he flinches, though he is hurrying on;
sentences.n: What stops the lion. θαμέες ‘close-set, thick’ describes the ἄκοντες ‘javelins’, ἀντίον ‘against him, in his face’ goes with ἀΐσσουσι ‘dart’, and θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν is ‘from bold hands’ (the feminine genitive plural in -άων). δεταί is a rare word, taken as ‘torches’ from the context, since they are burning (καιόμεναι) and the lion shrinks from them. τάς τε is a relative (‘which’), τρεῖ is ‘he flinches’ (τρέω, as at 546), and ἐσσύμενος περ is ‘hurrying though he is’, the participle of σεύομαι with the concessive περ.

sentences.t: ἠῶθεν δ’ ἀπὸ νόσφιν ἔβη τετιηότι θυμῷ·
sentences.tr: ēōthen d’ apo nosphin ebē tetiēoti thymōi·
sentences.l: and at dawn away, apart, he went with grieved heart;
sentences.i: and at dawn he goes off, away, grieved at heart;
sentences.n: The lion goes away. ἠῶθεν ‘at dawn’ (the suffix -θεν), ἀπὸ … νόσφιν ‘away and apart’; ἔβη is the aorist of βαίνω, an aorist of a simile like those above, and τετιηότι is the perfect participle of a verb for grieving, agreeing with θυμῷ (‘with a grieved heart’).

sentences.t:
ὣς Αἴας τότ’ ἀπὸ Τρώων τετιημένος ἦτορ
ἤϊε πόλλ’ ἀέκων·
sentences.tr:
hōs Aias tot’ apo Trōōn tetiēmenos ētor
ēïe poll’ aekōn·
sentences.l:
So Ajax then from the Trojans, grieved in heart,
went, much unwilling;
sentences.i: So then Ajax went away from the Trojans, grieved at heart, very unwilling;
sentences.n: The comparison is made: ὣς … τότε ‘so then’ turns from the lion to Ajax. τετιημένος ἦτορ ‘grieved in the heart’ has an accusative of respect, and ἤϊε is the Homeric imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (Attic ᾔει). πόλλ’ is πολλά used as an adverb (‘greatly’), and ἀέκων is ‘unwilling’.

sentences.t: περὶ γὰρ δίε νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: peri gar die nēusin Achaiōn.
sentences.l: for greatly he feared for the ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: for he was deeply afraid for the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: This tells why he is unwilling. περί … δίε is ‘feared exceedingly’: περί is an adverb ‘exceedingly’ here, and δίε is an epic past tense of the verb of fear (the stem of δείδω, δέος). The dative νηυσίν ‘for the ships’ says what he fears for.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ὄνος παρ’ ἄρουραν ἰὼν ἐβιήσατο παῖδας
νωθής, ᾧ δὴ πολλὰ περὶ ῥόπαλ’ ἀμφὶς ἐάγῃ,
κείρει τ’ εἰσελθὼν βαθὺ λήϊον·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ onos par’ arouran iōn ebiēsato paidas
nōthēs, hōi dē polla peri rhopal’ amphis eagēi,
keirei t’ eiselthōn bathy lēïon·
sentences.i: And as when a sluggish ass, going along beside a field, gets the better of boys, and many clubs are broken round him on every side, and he goes in and crops the deep standing crop;
sentences.n: A second simile for Ajax. ὄνος is an ass, νωθής ‘sluggish’ (the word gives the beast’s slowness and stubbornness), and ἐβιήσατο is the aorist of βιάομαι ‘overpower, get the better of’, again the aorist of a simile. ᾧ is a relative ‘on whom’, and ῥόπαλ’ is ῥόπαλα ‘clubs’; ἐάγῃ is the aorist passive subjunctive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’; περί and ἀμφίς both mean ‘round about’, so the clubs break all around him. κείρει ‘crops’ (as one shears) has εἰσελθών ‘going in’, and βαθὺ λήϊον is the ‘deep standing crop’, thick grain that stands in the field.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ τε παῖδες
τύπτουσιν ῥοπάλοισι·
sentences.tr:
hoi de te paides
typtousin rhopaloisi·
sentences.l:
and the boys
strike him with clubs;
sentences.i: while the boys strike him with clubs;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ τε ‘but they’ turns to the boys (παῖδες). τύπτουσιν is ‘strike’, and ῥοπάλοισι is the dative plural in -οισι of ῥόπαλον ‘club’.

sentences.t: βίη δέ τε νηπίη αὐτῶν·
sentences.tr: biē de te nēpiē autōn·
sentences.l: but childish is their strength;
sentences.i: but their strength is a child’s;
sentences.n: βίη … νηπίη αὐτῶν ‘their strength is childish’: νηπίη is the adjective of νήπιος (‘infant, childish’) and αὐτῶν ‘of them’ is the boys. δέ τε is ‘but’ with the epic τε.

sentences.t: σπουδῇ τ’ ἐξήλασσαν, ἐπεί τ’ ἐκορέσσατο φορβῆς·
sentences.tr: spoudēi t’ exēlassan, epei t’ ekoressato phorbēs·
sentences.l: and with difficulty they drove him out, when he had had his fill of fodder;
sentences.i: and only with difficulty do they drive him out, once he has had his fill of fodder;
sentences.n: σπουδῇ is ‘with difficulty’ (as the table has it), ἐξήλασσαν the aorist of ἐξελαύνω ‘drive out’, and ἐκορέσσατο the aorist middle of κορέννυμι ‘have one’s fill’, with the genitive φορβῆς ‘fodder, food’. The two τε are the epic τε.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότ’ ἔπειτ’ Αἴαντα μέγαν Τελαμώνιον υἱὸν
Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι πολυηγερέες τ’ ἐπίκουροι
νύσσοντες ξυστοῖσι μέσον σάκος αἰὲν ἕποντο.
sentences.tr:
hōs tot’ epeit’ Aianta megan Telamōnion huion
Trōes hyperthymoi polyēgerees t’ epikouroi
nyssontes xystoisi meson sakos aien heponto.
sentences.l:
So then, thereupon, Ajax, great Telamonian son,
the high-spirited Trojans and the many-gathered allies
stabbing with polished spears the shield in the middle always followed.
sentences.i: So then the high-spirited Trojans and their allies, gathered in great numbers, always followed Ajax, Telamon’s great son, stabbing the middle of his shield with polished spears.
sentences.n: The simile closes on Ajax. Αἴαντα is the object of ἕποντο, the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ without its augment, and μέγαν Τελαμώνιον υἱόν ‘great Telamonian son’ is the adjective ‘of Telamon’ with ‘son’, and αἰέν ‘always’ goes with ἕποντο, not with νύσσοντες. ὑπέρθυμοι is ‘high-spirited’, and ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’. πολυηγερέες is a rare word built on πολύς + ἀγείρω ‘gather’, ‘gathered in great numbers’ or ‘from many places’, which the form alone does not settle. νύσσοντες is ‘stabbing’, ξυστοῖσι the dative plural of ξυστόν, a spear with a smoothed shaft, and μέσον σάκος the middle of the shield, the part stabbed.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ἄλλοτε μὲν μνησάσκετο θούριδος ἀλκῆς
αὖτις ὑποστρεφθείς, καὶ ἐρητύσασκε φάλαγγας
Τρώων ἱπποδάμων·
sentences.tr:
Aias d’ allote men mnēsasketo thouridos alkēs
autis hypostrephtheis, kai erētysaske phalangas
Trōōn hippodamōn·
sentences.i: At times Ajax would remember impetuous might, turning round again, and would check the battle-lines of the Trojans, tamers of horses;
sentences.n: Ajax now fights as he goes. ἄλλοτε μέν ‘at one time’ is answered by ὁτὲ δέ ‘at another’ in the next unit, and the three verbs μνησάσκετο, ἐρητύσασκε, τρωπάσκετο carry the suffix -σκ-, which makes them repeated actions (‘would …’). μνησάσκετο θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘was mindful of impetuous might’ is the formula for turning his mind to fighting-strength (μιμνήσκομαι takes the genitive). ὑποστρεφθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὑποστρέφω ‘turn round’. ἐρητύσασκε is ‘would restrain’, φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’, and ἱπποδάμων ‘horse-taming’ is the epithet of the Trojans.

sentences.t: ὁτὲ δὲ τρωπάσκετο φεύγειν.
sentences.tr: hote de trōpasketo pheugein.
sentences.l: and at another time would turn to flee.
sentences.i: and at other times would turn and flee.
sentences.n: ὁτέ is the form of ὅτε ‘at the time when’ used as ‘at another time’, balancing ἄλλοτε μέν of the last unit. τρωπάσκετο is the repeated form of τρωπάω (a frequentative of τρέπω ‘turn’), ‘would turn himself’, and φεύγειν is the infinitive ‘to flee’.

sentences.t:
πάντας δὲ προέεργε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας ὁδεύειν,
αὐτὸς δὲ Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν θῦνε μεσηγὺ
ἱστάμενος·
sentences.tr:
pantas de proeerge thoas epi nēas hodeuein,
autos de Trōōn kai Achaiōn thyne mesēgy
histamenos·
sentences.i: He kept them all from advancing to the swift ships, and he himself rushed between the Trojans and the Achaeans, taking his stand there;
sentences.n: προέεργε is the imperfect of προείργω ‘keep back, bar’, with the infinitive ὁδεύειν ‘to march’. πάντας ‘all’ is the Trojans, who are not named until the next line. θῦνε is ‘rushed’ (θύνω), μεσηγύ ‘between’ takes the genitive, and the participle ἱστάμενος ‘taking his stand’ stands beside θῦνε, two things that seem to pull apart; the English keeps both.

sentences.t:
τὰ δὲ δοῦρα θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν
ἄλλα μὲν ἐν σάκεϊ μεγάλῳ πάγεν ὄρμενα πρόσσω,
πολλὰ δὲ καὶ μεσσηγύ, πάρος χρόα λευκὸν ἐπαυρεῖν,
ἐν γαίῃ ἵσταντο λιλαιόμενα χροὸς ἆσαι.
sentences.tr:
ta de doura thraseiaōn apo cheirōn
alla men en sakeï megalōi pagen ormena prossō,
polla de kai messēgy, paros chroa leukon epaurein,
en gaiēi histanto lilaiomena chroos asai.
sentences.l:
and the spears from bold hands,
some in the great shield stuck, speeding forward,
but many also midway, before the white flesh to touch,
in the earth stood, longing to glut themselves with flesh.
sentences.i: As for the spears from bold hands, some stuck in the great shield as they sped forward, but many stood in the earth midway, before they could touch his white flesh, longing to glut themselves on it.
sentences.n: τὰ … δοῦρα ‘those spears’ is the subject, with θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν ‘from bold hands’ as at 553. ἄλλα μέν … πολλὰ δέ means ‘some … but many’. πάγεν is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix, stick’ without its augment, and ὄρμενα is a participle of ὄρνυμι (‘speeding’). μεσσηγύ is ‘midway’ (the same word as μεσηγύ at 570), and πάρος … ἐπαυρεῖν ‘before touching’ is πάρος with an infinitive; ἐπαυρεῖν is ‘touch, get at’. The spears are spoken of as if they wanted something: λιλαιόμενα ‘longing’ with the aorist infinitive ἆσαι ‘to glut’, which takes the genitive χροὸς ‘flesh’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησ’ Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱὸς
Εὐρύπυλος πυκινοῖσι βιαζόμενον βελέεσσι,
στῆ ῥα παρ’ αὐτὸν ἰών, καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ,
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun enoēs’ Euaimonos aglaos huios
Eurypylos pykinoisi biazomenon beleessi,
stē rha par’ auton iōn, kai akontise douri phaeinōi,
sentences.l:
Him then as he noticed, Euaemon’s splendid son,
Eurypylus, pressed hard by thick shafts,
stood beside him, coming up, and hurled with a shining spear,
sentences.i: And when Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son, noticed him hard pressed by thick shafts, he came up and stood beside him, and hurled his shining spear,
sentences.n: A new scene, with Eurypylus as its subject. τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησ’ ‘and when he noticed him’ is the opening formula that gives a new subject; the man noticed is Ajax (βιαζόμενον, passive of βιάζω ‘press hard’, with πυκινοῖσι βελέεσσι ‘thick shafts’). στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, ῥα is the particle, and ἰών ‘coming up’ the participle of εἶμι. ἀκόντισε is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω ‘hurl a javelin’, and δουρὶ φαεινῷ ‘a shining spear’ the instrument.

sentences.t:
καὶ βάλε Φαυσιάδην Ἀπισάονα ποιμένα λαῶν
ἧπαρ ὑπὸ πραπίδων, εἶθαρ δ’ ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν·
sentences.tr:
kai bale Phausiadēn Apisaona poimena laōn
hēpar hypo prapidōn, eithar d’ hypo gounat’ elysen·
sentences.l:
and struck Phausias’-son Apisaon, shepherd of the people,
in the liver beneath the midriff, and at once he loosed his knees;
sentences.i: and hit Apisaon, son of Phausias, shepherd of the people, in the liver under the midriff, and at once loosed his knees;
sentences.n: βάλε is the aorist of βάλλω without its augment, ‘struck, hit’; Φαυσιάδην is the patronymic ‘son of Phausias’, and ποιμένα λαῶν the stock ‘shepherd of the people’. ἧπαρ ‘liver’ is the place struck, and πραπίδων is the genitive of πραπίδες, which elsewhere means the ‘wits’ but here is the physical midriff. ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν ‘he loosed the knees from under him’ is the idiom for killing (a man whose knees are loosed falls dead); ὑπό is in tmesis and εἶθαρ means ‘at once’.

sentences.t: Εὐρύπυλος δ’ ἐπόρουσε καὶ αἴνυτο τεύχε’ ἀπ’ ὤμων.
sentences.tr: Eurypylos d’ eporouse kai ainyto teuche’ ap’ ōmōn.
sentences.l: And Eurypylus sprang upon him and was taking the armour from his shoulders.
sentences.i: Then Eurypylus sprang upon him and began to strip the armour from his shoulders.
sentences.n: ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘spring upon’, and αἴνυτο the imperfect of αἴνυμαι ‘take’, so the action is begun and not finished. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’, and ἀπ’ ὤμων is ‘from his shoulders’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδὴς
τεύχε’ ἀπαινύμενον Ἀπισάονος, αὐτίκα τόξον
ἕλκετ’ ἐπ’ Εὐρυπύλῳ, καί μιν βάλε μηρὸν ὀϊστῷ
δεξιόν·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun enoēsen Alexandros theoeidēs
teuche’ apainymenon Apisaonos, autika toxon
helket’ ep’ Eurypylōi, kai min bale mēron oïstōi
dexion·
sentences.l:
Him then as he noticed, Alexander godlike-in-form,
stripping the armour from Apisaon, at once the bow
he drew against Eurypylus, and struck him in the thigh with an arrow,
the right one;
sentences.i: And when Alexander, godlike in form, noticed him stripping the armour from Apisaon, he at once drew his bow against Eurypylus, and hit him with an arrow in the right thigh;
sentences.n: Line 581 is 3.30 word for word, and 585 below is 3.32. τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν again passes the action to a new man, Alexander (Paris), who has the epithet θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ (θεός + εἶδος ‘form’). ἀπαινύμενον is the present participle of ἀπαίνυμαι ‘strip, take from’, with the genitive of the man stripped, Ἀπισάονος. ἕλκετ’ is ἕλκετο, the imperfect middle of ἕλκω ‘draw’, and ἐπ’ Εὐρυπύλῳ ‘against Eurypylus’. μιν is ‘him’, and μηρὸν … δεξιόν is ‘the right thigh’, with ὀϊστῷ the dative ‘with an arrow’.

sentences.t: ἐκλάσθη δὲ δόναξ, ἐβάρυνε δὲ μηρόν.
sentences.tr: eklasthē de donax, ebaryne de mēron.
sentences.l: and the reed was broken, and it weighed the thigh down.
sentences.i: and the shaft snapped, and it weighed his thigh down.
sentences.n: ἐκλάσθη is the aorist passive of κλάω ‘break’. δόναξ is ‘reed’, here the reed shaft of the arrow. ἐβάρυνε ‘weighed down’ has no subject stated: the broken arrow that is still in the thigh or the wound itself would fit, and the English keeps a bare ‘it’.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων,
ἤϋσεν δὲ διαπρύσιον Δαναοῖσι γεγωνώς·
sentences.tr:
aps d’ hetarōn eis ethnos echazeto kēr’ aleeinōn,
ēÿsen de diaprysion Danaoisi gegōnōs·
sentences.l:
and back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding,
and he shouted piercingly, calling to the Danaans:
sentences.i: He drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death, and shouted piercingly, calling out to the Danaans:
sentences.n: Line 585 is 3.32 and line 586 is 8.227, both word for word. The subject, not named, is Eurypylus, the man just hit. ἂψ ‘back’, ἔθνος ‘company’ (a body of people), ἐχάζετο ‘was drawing away’ (χάζομαι), and κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων ‘avoiding death-fate’, with κῆρ’ as κῆρα, the death-fate that carries a man off and not the κῆρ ‘heart’. ἤϋσεν is ‘shouted’ (an aorist, with the diaeresis the edition prints); διαπρύσιον ‘piercingly’ is an adverb, and γεγωνώς ‘calling out’ the perfect participle of γεγωνέω.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
στῆτ’ ἐλελιχθέντες καὶ ἀμύνετε νηλεὲς ἦμαρ
Αἴανθ’, ὃς βελέεσσι βιάζεται, οὐδέ ἕ φημι
φεύξεσθ’ ἐκ πολέμοιο δυσηχέος·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi Argeiōn hēgētores ēde medontes
stēt’ elelichthentes kai amynete nēlees ēmar
Aianth’, hos beleessi biazetai, oude he phēmi
pheuxesth’ ek polemoio dysēcheos·
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
stand, whirled round, and ward off the pitiless day
from Ajax, who is hard pressed by shafts, and I say he will not
escape from the ill-sounding war;
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives, wheel round and stand, and ward the pitiless day off Ajax, who is hard pressed by shafts; and I say he will not escape from the ill-sounding war;
sentences.n: Line 587 is 2.79 word for word. Eurypylus calls on the Argive chiefs. ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’, ἡγήτορες ‘leaders’, μέδοντες ‘lords’. στῆτ’ is the aorist imperative of ἵστημι ‘stand’ and ἐλελιχθέντες the aorist passive participle of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl round’, so ‘wheeling round’; ἀμύνετε is ‘ward off’, with νηλεὲς ἦμαρ ‘the pitiless day’ as what is warded off and Αἴανθ’ (Αἴαντα elided, as at 544) the man it threatens. ὃς βελέεσσι βιάζεται is ‘who is hard pressed by shafts’, and οὐδέ ἕ φημι φεύξεσθ’ is ‘and I say he will not escape’, a future infinitive with ἕ ‘him’. πολέμοιο δυσηχέος ‘ill-sounding war’ has the table’s rendering of δυσηχής.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἄντην
ἵστασθ’ ἀμφ’ Αἴαντα μέγαν Τελαμώνιον υἱόν.
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ antēn
histasth’ amph’ Aianta megan Telamōnion huion.
sentences.l:
but right in front
stand around Ajax, great Telamonian son.”
sentences.i: but take your stand right in front, around Ajax, Telamon’s great son.”
sentences.n: ἄντην ‘right in front’ (here, facing the enemy) goes with the middle imperative ἵστασθ’ ‘take your stand’, and ἀμφ’ Αἴαντα is ‘around Ajax’. μέγαν Τελαμώνιον υἱόν is the same phrase as at 563. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ Εὐρύπυλος βεβλημένος· οἳ δὲ παρ’ αὐτὸν
πλησίοι ἔστησαν σάκε’ ὤμοισι κλίναντες
δούρατ’ ἀνασχόμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’ Eurypylos beblēmenos· hoi de par’ auton
plēsioi estēsan sake’ ōmoisi klinantes
dourat’ anaschomenoi·
sentences.i: So spoke the wounded Eurypylus; and they stood close beside him, resting their shields against their shoulders and holding up their spears;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is the formula that closes a speech, and βεβλημένος is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω, ‘struck, wounded’. οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Argive leaders he has called on, and αὐτόν ‘him’ is Eurypylus (Ajax is not yet with them, since he comes to them in the next unit). πλησίοι is ‘close’, σάκε’ is σάκεα ‘shields’ and ὤμοισι the dative of ὦμος ‘shoulder’; κλίναντες is ‘leaning’, and δούρατ’ ἀνασχόμενοι the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω, ‘holding up spears’ (δούρατ’ is the accusative plural of δόρυ).

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ ἀντίος ἤλυθεν Αἴας.
sentences.tr: tōn d’ antios ēlythen Aias.
sentences.l: and opposite them came Ajax.
sentences.i: and Ajax came to meet them.
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of them’ depends on ἀντίος ‘opposite, facing’, and ἤλυθεν is the epic form of ἦλθεν ‘came’. Ajax moves toward the men who have gathered to help him.

sentences.t: στῆ δὲ μεταστρεφθείς, ἐπεὶ ἵκετο ἔθνος ἑταίρων.
sentences.tr: stē de metastrephtheis, epei hiketo ethnos hetairōn.
sentences.l: And he stood, having turned about, when he reached the company of his companions.
sentences.i: He turned about and stood when he reached the company of his companions.
sentences.n: στῆ δὲ μεταστρεφθείς ‘and he stood, having turned about’, with μεταστρεφθείς the aorist passive participle of μεταστρέφω ‘turn round’ (the Greek puts the standing first; the English puts the turning first, as it happened). ἵκετο is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’ without its augment, and ἔθνος ἑταίρων is ‘the company of companions’, as at 585. The ‘he’ is Ajax.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν μάρναντο δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men marnanto demas pyros aithomenoio·
sentences.l: So they, for their part, fought in the likeness of blazing fire;
sentences.i: So they fought, like a blazing fire;
sentences.n: οἳ μέν ‘they, for their part’ awaits the δέ of Νέστορα δ’ in the next line. μάρναντο is ‘fought’ (the imperfect of μάρναμαι), and δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο is ‘in the likeness of blazing fire’ (δέμας ‘body, form’ is used as an adverbial accusative, and αἰθομένοιο the genitive of the participle of αἴθω).

sentences.t:
Νέστορα δ’ ἐκ πολέμοιο φέρον Νηλήϊαι ἵπποι
ἱδρῶσαι, ἦγον δὲ Μαχάονα ποιμένα λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
Nestora d’ ek polemoio pheron Nēlēïai hippoi
hidrōsai, ēgon de Machaona poimena laōn.
sentences.l:
but Nestor out of the war carried the Neleian horses,
sweating, and they were bringing Machaon, shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: But the Neleian horses were carrying Nestor out of the war, in a sweat, and bringing Machaon, shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: The scene changes to the other wing. Νηλήϊαι ἵπποι are the ‘Neleian horses’, called after Neleus, Nestor’s father (the adjective Νηλήϊος ‘of Neleus’). φέρον and ἦγον are imperfects, ‘were carrying’ and ‘were bringing’, and ἱδρῶσαι is the feminine participle of ἱδρόω ‘sweat’. Μαχάονα ποιμένα λαῶν is Machaon, wounded in the last part, with the stock ‘shepherd of the people’.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ἐνόησε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton de idōn enoēse podarkēs dios Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him, having seen, noticed swift-footed, heavenly Achilles;
sentences.i: Swift-footed, heavenly Achilles saw him and took note of him;
sentences.n: τὸν … ἰδών ‘having seen him’ with ἐνόησε ‘noticed’ (an aorist) is a pair: he saw and took note. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the stock phrase ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’ (ποδάρκης is probably πούς + ἀρκέω, the formation not secure). The man seen is the one just named, Machaon.

sentences.t:
ἑστήκει γὰρ ἐπὶ πρυμνῇ μεγακήτεϊ νηῒ
εἰσορόων πόνον αἰπὺν ἰῶκά τε δακρυόεσσαν.
sentences.tr:
hestēkei gar epi prymnēi megakēteï nēï
eisoroōn ponon aipyn iōka te dakryoessan.
sentences.l:
for he was standing on the stern of the huge ship,
looking at the steep toil and the tearful rush.
sentences.i: for he was standing on the stern of his huge ship, looking at the steep toil and the tearful rush.
sentences.n: ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘was standing’, and γάρ explains how he saw. πρυμνῇ is the ‘stern’ (taken as a noun here; it can also be ‘hindmost’), and μεγακήτεϊ ‘huge’ is the table’s rendering (it is probably μέγα- + κῆτος ‘sea-monster’, but the formation is not secure). εἰσορόων is ‘looking at’, πόνον αἰπύν ‘steep toil’, and ἰῶκα is a rare word whose exact sense is not known (it seems to be the rush of battle, and the later glosses connect it with διώκω ‘pursue’), so the English says only ‘rush’; δακρυόεσσαν is ‘tearful’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἑταῖρον ἑὸν Πατροκλῆα προσέειπε
φθεγξάμενος παρὰ νηός·
sentences.tr:
aipsa d’ hetairon heon Patroklēa proseeipe
phthenxamenos para nēos·
sentences.l:
And at once to his own companion Patroclus he spoke,
calling out from beside the ship;
sentences.i: and at once, calling out from beside the ship, he spoke to his own companion Patroclus;
sentences.n: Achilles calls to Patroclus. ἑταῖρον ἑὸν is ‘his own companion’: ἑόν is the possessive ὅς (‘his own’), not the relative. προσέειπε is ‘addressed’ (the epic form of προσεῖπε), φθεγξάμενος the aorist participle of φθέγγομαι ‘call out’, and παρὰ νηός ‘from beside the ship’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ κλισίηθεν ἀκούσας
ἔκμολεν ἶσος Ἄρηϊ, κακοῦ δ’ ἄρα οἱ πέλεν ἀρχή.
sentences.tr:
ho de klisiēthen akousas
ekmolen isos Arēï, kakou d’ ara hoi pelen archē.
sentences.l:
and he, hearing from the hut,
came out, equal to Ares, and for him then the beginning of evil it was.
sentences.i: and he heard him from the hut and came out, the equal of Ares, and that was the beginning of evil for him.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Patroclus. κλισίηθεν is ‘from the hut’ (the suffix -θεν) and ἀκούσας the aorist participle ‘having heard’. ἔκμολεν is the aorist of βλώσκω ‘go, come’ with ἐκ ‘out’, and ἶσος Ἄρηϊ ‘equal to Ares’ compares him to the war-god. κακοῦ δ’ ἄρα οἱ πέλεν ἀρχή is ‘and for him it was the beginning of evil’: πέλεν is the imperfect of πέλω ‘be’ without its augment and οἱ ‘for him’; the poet looks ahead here.

sentences.t: τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton proteros proseeipe Menoitiou alkimos huios·
sentences.l: Him first addressed Menoetius’ sturdy son:
sentences.i: Menoetius’ sturdy son spoke to him first:
sentences.n: This is the whole-line speech introduction with πρότερος προσέειπε. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός is Patroclus, called ‘sturdy’ (ἄλκιμος, from ἀλκή ‘might’), and πρότερος ‘first’ says that he speaks before Achilles has told him what he wants.

sentences.t: τίπτέ με κικλήσκεις Ἀχιλεῦ;
sentences.tr: tipte me kiklēskeis Achileu;
sentences.l: “Why do you call me, Achilles?
sentences.i: “Why are you calling me, Achilles?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why, then’, κικλήσκεις ‘you call, summon’ is a present with a reduplicated stem (a form of καλέω), and Ἀχιλεῦ is the vocative of Ἀχιλλεύς.

sentences.t: τί δέ σε χρεὼ ἐμεῖο;
sentences.tr: ti de se chreō emeio;
sentences.l: and what need of me is upon you?”
sentences.i: What do you need me for?”
sentences.n: τί δέ σε χρεὼ ἐμεῖο: χρεώ ‘need’ has the person in need in the accusative (σε ‘you’) and the thing needed in the genitive (ἐμεῖο, the epic genitive of ἐγώ ‘me’). The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula, the same line as 1.84. ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the present participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’ has the accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
δῖε Μενοιτιάδη τῷ ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ
νῦν ὀΐω περὶ γούνατ’ ἐμὰ στήσεσθαι Ἀχαιοὺς
λισσομένους·
sentences.tr:
die Menoitiadē tōi emōi kecharismene thymōi
nyn oïō peri gounat’ ema stēsesthai Achaious
lissomenous·
sentences.i: “Heavenly son of Menoetius, dear to my heart, now I think the Achaeans will stand about my knees, entreating;
sentences.n: Achilles looks ahead to the Achaeans coming to him as suppliants. δῖε is the vocative of δῖος ‘heavenly’, and Μενοιτιάδη the patronymic vocative ‘son of Menoetius’. τῷ ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ is ‘made welcome to my heart’ (κεχαρισμένε, the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι, in the vocative; τῷ ἐμῷ … θυμῷ is ‘to my heart’). ὀΐω is ‘I think’, with the infinitive στήσεσθαι (future middle of ἵστημι, ‘will stand’) and the accusative Ἀχαιούς. περὶ γούνατ’ ἐμά is ‘about my knees’, the knees a suppliant touches, and λισσομένους the participle ‘entreating’.

sentences.t: χρειὼ γὰρ ἱκάνεται οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτός.
sentences.tr: chreiō gar hikanetai ouket’ anektos.
sentences.l: for need is coming, no longer bearable.
sentences.i: for a need is coming upon them that can no longer be borne.
sentences.n: χρειώ is the epic spelling of χρεώ ‘need’ (606), ἱκάνεται is ‘comes to, reaches’ (the ‘them’ is the Achaeans, left unsaid), and οὐκέτ’ ἀνεκτός is ‘no longer bearable’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν Πάτροκλε Διῒ φίλε Νέστορ’ ἔρειο
ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγει βεβλημένον ἐκ πολέμοιο·
sentences.tr:
all’ ithi nyn Patrokle Diï phile Nestor’ ereio
hon tina touton agei beblēmenon ek polemoio·
sentences.l:
But go now, Patroclus, dear to Zeus, ask Nestor
whoever this man is whom he is bringing, struck, out of the war;
sentences.i: But go now, Patroclus, dear to Zeus, and ask Nestor who this is whom he is bringing out of the war, wounded;
sentences.n: Διῒ φίλε is ‘dear to Zeus’ (the dative Διΐ, with its diaeresis, and the vocative φίλε). ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’; ἔρειο is the aorist imperative middle of ἔρομαι ‘ask’, and Νέστορ’ is Νέστορα elided. ὅν τινα τοῦτον is an indirect question, ‘whoever this man is whom’, with ἄγει ‘he is bringing’ and βεβλημένον ‘struck, wounded’, the perfect passive participle of βάλλω.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μὲν τά γ’ ὄπισθε Μαχάονι πάντα ἔοικε
τῷ Ἀσκληπιάδῃ, ἀτὰρ οὐκ ἴδον ὄμματα φωτός·
sentences.tr:
ētoi men ta g’ opisthe Machaoni panta eoike
tōi Asklēpiadēi, atar ouk idon ommata phōtos·
sentences.l:
Indeed, in the parts behind, in all things he is like Machaon,
the Asclepius’-son, but I did not see the eyes of the man;
sentences.i: From behind he looks in everything like Machaon, son of Asclepius, but I did not see the man’s eyes;
sentences.n: ἤτοι (one word in this edition) with μέν looks ahead to the contrast with ἀτάρ ‘but’. τά γ’ ὄπισθε is ‘the parts behind’, an accusative of respect, and ἔοικε ‘is like’ takes the dative Μαχάονι, with πάντα ‘in all things’. Ἀσκληπιάδῃ is the patronymic ‘son of Asclepius’, with τῷ the article in its demonstrative force (‘that son of Asclepius’). ἴδον is the aorist of ὁράω without its augment, and ὄμματα φωτός is ‘the man’s eyes’ (φώς, φωτός ‘man’).

sentences.t: ἵπποι γάρ με παρήϊξαν πρόσσω μεμαυῖαι.
sentences.tr: hippoi gar me parēïxan prossō memauiai.
sentences.l: for the horses rushed past me forward, eager.”
sentences.i: for the horses rushed past me, eager to go forward.”
sentences.n: ἵπποι γάρ gives the reason he did not see the man’s eyes. παρήϊξαν is the aorist of παραΐσσω ‘rush past’, πρόσσω ‘forward’, and μεμαυῖαι the feminine perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, agreeing with ἵπποι. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Πάτροκλος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθεθ’ ἑταίρῳ,
βῆ δὲ θέειν παρά τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Patroklos de philōi epepeitheth’ hetairōi,
bē de theein para te klisias kai nēas Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Patroclus obeyed his dear companion,
and went to run along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Patroclus obeyed his dear companion, and set off running along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Line 616 is 1.345 word for word. ἐπεπείθεθ’ (= ἐπεπείθετο) is an epic imperfect of πείθομαι ‘obey’ with the dative φίλῳ ἑταίρῳ. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω, and βῆ … θέειν ‘went to run’ is the epic way of saying ‘set off running’ (θέειν, the uncontracted infinitive of θέω). παρά τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας is ‘along the huts and the ships’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ κλισίην Νηληϊάδεω ἀφίκοντο,
αὐτοὶ μέν ῥ’ ἀπέβησαν ἐπὶ χθόνα πουλυβότειραν,
ἵππους δ’ Εὐρυμέδων θεράπων λύε τοῖο γέροντος
ἐξ ὀχέων·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē klisiēn Nēlēïadeō aphikonto,
autoi men rh’ apebēsan epi chthona poulyboteiran,
hippous d’ Eurymedōn therapōn lye toio gerontos
ex ocheōn·
sentences.l:
And when they came to the hut of Neleus’-son,
they themselves stepped down upon the much-nourishing earth,
and the horses Eurymedon, the attendant, loosed, of the old man,
from the chariot;
sentences.i: And when they came to the hut of Neleus’ son, they themselves stepped down onto the earth that feeds so many, and Eurymedon, the old man’s attendant, unyoked the horses from the chariot;
sentences.n: Patroclus is still running; οἳ δ’ ‘they’ are Nestor and Machaon, arrived at Nestor’s hut. Νηληϊάδεω is the patronymic in -εω, ‘of Neleus’ son’ (Nestor). ἀπέβησαν is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω ‘step down’, and πουλυβότειραν ‘much-nourishing’ is the epithet of the earth (the table’s). θεράπων ‘attendant’ is Eurymedon, and τοῖο γέροντος ‘of the old man’ has τοῖο, the Homeric genitive of the article-form. ἐξ ὀχέων is plural for the single chariot (‘from the chariot’).

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἱδρῶ ἀπεψύχοντο χιτώνων
στάντε ποτὶ πνοιὴν παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός·
sentences.tr:
toi d’ hidrō apepsychonto chitōnōn
stante poti pnoiēn para thin’ halos·
sentences.l:
and they were cooling off the sweat from their tunics,
standing the two to the breeze, by the shore of the sea;
sentences.i: and the two of them stood facing the breeze by the shore of the sea and cooled the sweat off their tunics;
sentences.n: τοί here is ‘they’ (the article-form as a pronoun): Nestor and Machaon, the two, as the dual participle στάντε ‘standing’ shows. ἀπεψύχοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀποψύχω ‘cool off, dry off’, with ἱδρῶ the accusative of ἱδρώς ‘sweat’ and the genitive χιτώνων ‘from the tunics’. ποτὶ πνοιήν is ‘toward the breeze’ (ποτί = πρός), and παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός ‘by the shore of the sea’ (θῖν’ is θῖνα, accusative of θίς ‘shore’).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ἐς κλισίην ἐλθόντες ἐπὶ κλισμοῖσι κάθιζον.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita
es klisiēn elthontes epi klismoisi kathizon.
sentences.l:
but then,
having gone into the hut, upon seats they sat down.
sentences.i: And then they went into the hut and sat down on seats.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα ‘but then’ moves on to the next step. κλισίην is ‘hut’ (ἐς = εἰς), ἐλθόντες the aorist participle ‘having gone’, and κλισμοῖσι the dative plural of κλισμός ‘seat’. κάθιζον is the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ τεῦχε κυκειῶ ἐϋπλόκαμος Ἑκαμήδη,
τὴν ἄρετ’ ἐκ Τενέδοιο γέρων, ὅτε πέρσεν Ἀχιλλεύς,
θυγατέρ’ Ἀρσινόου μεγαλήτορος, ἥν οἱ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἔξελον οὕνεκα βουλῇ ἀριστεύεσκεν ἁπάντων.
sentences.tr:
toisi de teuche kykeiō eÿplokamos Hekamēdē,
tēn aret’ ek Tenedoio gerōn, hote persen Achilleus,
thygater’ Arsinoou megalētoros, hēn hoi Achaioi
exelon houneka boulēi aristeuesken hapantōn.
sentences.l:
And for them was making a stirred drink fine-plaited Hecamede,
whom the old man won for himself from Tenedos, when Achilles sacked it,
daughter of great-spirited Arsinous, whom for him the Achaeans
chose out, because in counsel he used to be the best of all.
sentences.i: And Hecamede, fine-plaited, was making them a mixed drink, the woman the old man had won from Tenedos when Achilles sacked it, the daughter of great-spirited Arsinous, whom the Achaeans chose out for him because he used to be the best of all in counsel.
sentences.n: Hecamede is introduced by who she is. Line 626 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρ’ is scanned long to fill the long place of the first foot, and the diphthong of οἱ is scanned short before the vowel after it. τεῦχε is the imperfect of τεύχω ‘make, prepare’, with τοῖσι ‘for them’; κυκειῶ is the accusative of κυκεών (the table’s ‘stirred drink’, ‘mixed drink’); ἐϋπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’ is the table’s. τήν is a relative ‘whom’, ἄρετ’ is ἄρετο, the aorist middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win for oneself’, and ὅτε πέρσεν Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘when Achilles sacked (it)’ (πέρθω). Ἀρσινόου is the genitive of Ἀρσίνοος, with the epithet μεγαλήτωρ ‘great-spirited’; οἱ is ‘for him’, ἔξελον the aorist of ἐξαιρέω ‘choose out’, and ἀριστεύεσκεν the repeated form of ἀριστεύω ‘be the best’, with βουλῇ ‘in counsel’ and the genitive ἁπάντων ‘of all’.

sentences.t:
ἥ σφωϊν πρῶτον μὲν ἐπιπροΐηλε τράπεζαν
καλὴν κυανόπεζαν ἐΰξοον, αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτῆς
χάλκειον κάνεον, ἐπὶ δὲ κρόμυον ποτῷ ὄψον,
sentences.tr:
hē sphōïn prōton men epiproïēle trapezan
kalēn kyanopezan eÿxoon, autar ep’ autēs
chalkeion kaneon, epi de kromyon potōi opson,
sentences.l:
She, for the two of them, first set out a table,
fair, dark-footed, well-polished, and upon it
a bronze basket, and on it an onion, a relish for the drink,
sentences.i: First she set out before them a fair table, dark-footed and well-polished, and on it a bronze basket, and on that an onion, a relish for the drink,
sentences.n: ἥ is ‘she’ (Hecamede), σφωϊν the dual dative ‘for the two of them’, and ἐπιπροΐηλε a rare verb meaning ‘set out before’ (the formation is not secure). πρῶτον μέν ‘first’ opens a list of what she sets on the table. κυανόπεζαν is ‘dark-footed’ (κυανο- is ‘dark’, as in κυανόπρῳρος ‘dark-prowed’, and πέζα here ‘foot’), ἐΰξοον ‘well-polished’ is the table’s, and κάνεον is a ‘basket’. κρόμυον is an ‘onion’, and ποτῷ ὄψον ‘a relish for the drink’ is something eaten along with it.

sentences.t:
ἠδὲ μέλι χλωρόν, παρὰ δ’ ἀλφίτου ἱεροῦ ἀκτήν,
πὰρ δὲ δέπας περικαλλές, ὃ οἴκοθεν ἦγ’ ὁ γεραιός,
χρυσείοις ἥλοισι πεπαρμένον·
sentences.tr:
ēde meli chlōron, para d’ alphitou hierou aktēn,
par de depas perikalles, ho oikothen ēg’ ho geraios,
chryseiois hēloisi peparmenon·
sentences.i: and yellow honey, and beside them the meal of sacred barley, and beside them a very fair cup that the old man had brought from home, set with golden studs;
sentences.n: The list goes on. μέλι χλωρόν is ‘yellow honey’ (the table’s), and ἀλφίτου ἱεροῦ ἀκτήν is ‘the meal of sacred barley’: ἀκτή here is ground grain, not the shore, and ἄλφιτον is barley-meal. δέπας περικαλλές is ‘a very fair cup’, ὃ οἴκοθεν ἦγ’ ὁ γεραιός ‘which the old man brought from home’ (οἴκοθεν, the suffix -θεν). χρυσείοις ἥλοισι πεπαρμένον is ‘pierced through with golden studs’, the perfect passive participle of πείρω, and ἦλος is a stud or nail.

sentences.t:
οὔατα δ’ αὐτοῦ
τέσσαρ’ ἔσαν, δοιαὶ δὲ πελειάδες ἀμφὶς ἕκαστον
χρύσειαι νεμέθοντο, δύω δ’ ὑπὸ πυθμένες ἦσαν.
sentences.tr:
ouata d’ autou
tessar’ esan, doiai de peleiades amphis hekaston
chryseiai nemethonto, dyō d’ hypo pythmenes ēsan.
sentences.l:
and its ears
were four, and two doves around each one,
golden, were feeding, and two bases beneath were.
sentences.i: It had four handles, and round each of them two golden doves were feeding, and there were two bases beneath.
sentences.n: The cup is described. οὔατα are ‘ears’, the word for the handles, and the English of the second layer says ‘handles’. πελειάδες are ‘doves’ and νεμέθοντο ‘were feeding’ (νεμέθομαι is a rare form of νέμομαι ‘graze’), with ἀμφὶς ἕκαστον ‘around each’; the Greek does not say whether it is two on each handle or one on each side. χρύσειαι is ‘golden’. δύω δ’ ὑπὸ πυθμένες ἦσαν is ‘and two bases were beneath’ (πυθμήν ‘bottom, base’); how a cup has two is not explained, and the English keeps the word.

sentences.t:
ἄλλος μὲν μογέων ἀποκινήσασκε τραπέζης
πλεῖον ἐόν, Νέστωρ δ’ ὁ γέρων ἀμογητὶ ἄειρεν.
sentences.tr:
allos men mogeōn apokinēsaske trapezēs
pleion eon, Nestōr d’ ho gerōn amogēti aeiren.
sentences.l:
Another, toiling, would move it from the table,
being full, but Nestor, the old man, lifted it without toil.
sentences.i: Another man would move it from the table only with toil, when it was full, but Nestor, the old man, lifted it without toil.
sentences.n: ἄλλος μέν … Νέστωρ δέ ‘another … but Nestor’. ἀποκινήσασκε is the repeated form of ἀποκινέω ‘move away’ (‘would move’), μογέων ‘toiling’ is the participle of μογέω, and πλεῖον ἐόν is ‘being full’ (ἐόν = ὄν). ἀμογητί ‘without toil’ is an adverb built on μογέω; ἄειρεν is the imperfect of ἀείρω ‘lift’. The cup’s weight is given to show how strong the old man is.

sentences.t:
ἐν τῷ ῥά σφι κύκησε γυνὴ ἐϊκυῖα θεῇσιν
οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ, ἐπὶ δ’ αἴγειον κνῆ τυρὸν
κνήστι χαλκείῃ, ἐπὶ δ’ ἄλφιτα λευκὰ πάλυνε,
πινέμεναι δ’ ἐκέλευσεν, ἐπεί ῥ’ ὥπλισσε κυκειῶ.
sentences.tr:
en tōi rha sphi kykēse gynē eïkuia theēisin
oinōi Pramneiōi, epi d’ aigeion knē tyron
knēsti chalkeiēi, epi d’ alphita leuka palyne,
pinemenai d’ ekeleusen, epei rh’ hōplisse kykeiō.
sentences.l:
In it for them stirred the woman, like goddesses,
with Pramnian wine, and over it goat’s cheese she grated
with a bronze grater, and over it white barley-meal she sprinkled,
and she ordered them to drink, when she had made ready the stirred drink.
sentences.i: In it the woman, like goddesses, stirred a drink for them with Pramnian wine, and grated goat’s cheese over it with a bronze grater, and sprinkled white barley-meal on top, and when she had made the drink ready she told them to drink.
sentences.n: ἐν τῷ is ‘in it’, the great cup of the last two units. κύκησε is the aorist of κυκάω ‘stir’, with σφι ‘for them’; γυνὴ ἐϊκυῖα θεῇσιν is ‘a woman like goddesses’ (ἐϊκυῖα the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα, θεῇσιν the dative plural of θεά). οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ is Pramnian wine, a named kind of wine. ἐπὶ … κνῆ is tmesis, ‘grated over’: κνῆ is a past tense of κνάω ‘grate’, with αἴγειον τυρόν ‘goat’s cheese’ and the dative κνήστι χαλκείῃ ‘with a bronze grater’. ἄλφιτα λευκά is ‘white barley-meal’, πάλυνε ‘sprinkled’, πινέμεναι the infinitive in -μεναι of πίνω (Attic πίνειν), and ὥπλισσε the aorist of ὁπλίζω ‘make ready’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν πίνοντ’ ἀφέτην πολυκαγκέα δίψαν
μύθοισιν τέρποντο πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἐνέποντες,
Πάτροκλος δὲ θύρῃσιν ἐφίστατο ἰσόθεος φώς.
sentences.tr:
tō d’ epei oun pinont’ aphetēn polykankea dipsan
mythoisin terponto pros allēlous enepontes,
Patroklos de thyrēisin ephistato isotheos phōs.
sentences.l:
And when the two, drinking, had put away their much-parching thirst,
with words they took their pleasure, speaking to one another,
and Patroclus at the doors stood, a man equal to a god.
sentences.i: And when the two of them had drunk and put away their parching thirst, they took their pleasure in speaking to one another, and Patroclus came and stood at the door, a man the equal of a god.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual ‘the two’ (Nestor and Machaon), and πίνοντ’ the dual participle ‘drinking’. ἀφέτην is the dual aorist of ἀφίημι ‘send away, put away’. πολυκαγκέα is a rare word, apparently ‘very parching’ (πολύ + a word for dry); its formation is not secure. μύθοισιν … τέρποντο is ‘took their pleasure with words’, with πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἐνέποντες ‘speaking to one another’. ἐφίστατο is the imperfect middle of ἐφίστημι ‘stand at’; θύρῃσιν is plural for the one door, and ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is the table’s phrase.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν ὁ γεραιὸς ἀπὸ θρόνου ὦρτο φαεινοῦ,
ἐς δ’ ἄγε χειρὸς ἑλών, κατὰ δ’ ἑδριάασθαι ἄνωγε.
sentences.tr:
ton de idōn ho geraios apo thronou ōrto phaeinou,
es d’ age cheiros helōn, kata d’ hedriaasthai anōge.
sentences.l:
And seeing him, the old man from his chair sprang up, shining,
and led him in, taking him by the hand, and to sit down he bade him.
sentences.i: The old man saw him and sprang up from his shining chair, and took him by the hand and led him in, and bade him sit down.
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ ἰδών ‘seeing him’ has Nestor as the subject (ὁ γεραιός ‘the old man’). ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘sprang up’, θρόνου φαεινοῦ ‘shining chair’. ἐς … ἄγε is tmesis, ‘led in’; χειρὸς ἑλών is ‘taking by the hand’ (the genitive for the part taken hold of), and κατὰ … ἑδριάασθαι ἄνωγε is ‘bade him sit down’: ἑδριάασθαι is the infinitive of ἑδριάομαι in its open form, and ἄνωγε the past of ἄνωγα ‘bid’.

sentences.t: Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀναίνετο εἶπέ τε μῦθον·
sentences.tr: Patroklos d’ heterōthen anaineto eipe te mython·
sentences.l: But Patroclus, from the other side, rejected it, and spoke a word:
sentences.i: But Patroclus, on his side, rejected the offer, and said:
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ answers Nestor’s pull on one side with Patroclus’ resistance on his. ἀναίνετο is the imperfect of ἀναίνομαι ‘reject’ (the Greek names no object; it is Nestor’s invitation to sit), and εἶπέ τε μῦθον ‘and spoke a word’ introduces the speech.

sentences.t: οὐχ ἕδος ἐστὶ γεραιὲ διοτρεφές, οὐδέ με πείσεις.
sentences.tr: ouch hedos esti geraie diotrephes, oude me peiseis.
sentences.l: “No seat is there, aged one, Zeus-nurtured one, and not me will you persuade.
sentences.i: “There is no sitting down, aged one, Zeus-nurtured one, and you will not persuade me.
sentences.n: ἕδος is ‘seat, sitting’, so οὐχ ἕδος ἐστί means that sitting is out of the question. γεραιὲ διοτρεφές is the table’s address ‘aged one, Zeus-nurtured one’ (διοτρεφής ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is an epithet of kings and old men). πείσεις is the future of πείθω ‘persuade’.

sentences.t:
αἰδοῖος νεμεσητὸς ὅ με προέηκε πυθέσθαι
ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγεις βεβλημένον·
sentences.tr:
aidoios nemesētos ho me proeēke pythesthai
hon tina touton ageis beblēmenon·
sentences.l:
Revered, quick to take offence, is he who sent me to learn
who this man is whom you bring, struck;
sentences.i: The man who sent me to find out who this is whom you are bringing, wounded, is a man to be revered, and quick to take offence;
sentences.n: αἰδοῖος νεμεσητός describes Achilles, who is not named. αἰδοῖος is ‘revered’ (the table’s) and νεμεσητός a word whose sense is disputed here (from νέμεσις ‘righteous indignation’): it is taken as ‘quick to take offence’. ὅ με προέηκε is ‘who sent me forth’ (the aorist of προίημι), πυθέσθαι ‘to learn’, and ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγεις βεβλημένον is the same indirect question as 612, now with ἄγεις ‘you bring’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς
γιγνώσκω, ὁρόω δὲ Μαχάονα ποιμένα λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
alla kai autos
gignōskō, horoō de Machaona poimena laōn.
sentences.l:
but I myself also
know, and I see Machaon, shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: but I know it myself as well, and I see Machaon, shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτός ‘but I myself also’. γιγνώσκω ‘I know (who he is)’ has its object left unsaid, and ὁρόω is the open form of ὁράω ‘see’, with Μαχάονα ποιμένα λαῶν as the man seen.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ ἔπος ἐρέων πάλιν ἄγγελος εἶμ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ.
sentences.tr: nyn de epos ereōn palin angelos eim’ Achilēï.
sentences.l: But now to tell the word, back as a messenger I shall go to Achilles.
sentences.i: But now I shall go back to Achilles as his messenger, to tell him the word.
sentences.n: ἔπος ἐρέων is ‘to tell the word’ (ἐρέων, a future participle of ἐρέω, expressing purpose), and εἶμ’ is εἶμι ‘I shall go’. ἄγγελος ‘messenger’ is in apposition to the subject, and Ἀχιλῆϊ is the Homeric dative of Ἀχιλλεύς.

sentences.t:
εὖ δὲ σὺ οἶσθα γεραιὲ διοτρεφές, οἷος ἐκεῖνος
δεινὸς ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr:
eu de sy oistha geraie diotrephes, hoios ekeinos
deinos anēr·
sentences.l:
And well you know, aged one, Zeus-nurtured one, what kind that one is,
a dread man;
sentences.i: And you know well, aged one, Zeus-nurtured one, what a man he is, a dread man;
sentences.n: εὖ … οἶσθα is ‘you know well’ (οἶσθα, the second singular of οἶδα), and οἷος ἐκεῖνος … ἀνήρ is ‘what kind of man that one is’, with δεινός ‘dread’ (the table’s) in apposition. ἐκεῖνος points at Achilles, who is not named.

sentences.t: τάχα κεν καὶ ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳτο.
sentences.tr: tacha ken kai anaition aitioōito.
sentences.l: quickly he might even blame one blameless.”
sentences.i: he might very soon blame even the blameless.”
sentences.n: τάχα κεν is ‘soon, perhaps’ with the optative, and αἰτιόῳτο is the third singular optative of αἰτιάομαι ‘blame’ in an open form. ἀναίτιον ‘blameless’ is the one who would be blamed; the Odyssey has the pair ἀναίτιον … αἰτιόῳο (second person) with ‘blameless’ and ‘blame’, and the English follows it. The speech ends here.
